lessons.title: The Three Pillars: Metrics, Logs & Traces

slots.practicalActivity: Pick any real running service you control (a side project, or even a lab VM from an earlier course) and write down 3 "known unknown" failure modes you'd build a monitoring check for, plus 1 realistic "unknown unknown" scenario an observable system would need to help you discover instead. Then, for that same service, write out concretely (not generically) what a metric, a log, and a trace would each look like for one real request it handles.
slots.deliverable: A written list of 3 known-unknown checks and 1 unknown-unknown scenario for a real service you control, plus concrete examples of what a metric, a log, and a trace would look like for one real request that service handles.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real SLI for a service you use or control (e.g. "percent of page loads under 2 seconds"), set a real SLO (e.g. 99.5% over 30 days), and do the actual arithmetic the lesson did: calculate the error budget in both percentage and approximate minutes-equivalent over a 30-day window. Then write one paragraph describing a hypothetical incident that would burn a specific amount of that budget, and whether the team would have room left to ship a risky change afterward.
slots.deliverable: A written SLI/SLO definition for a real service with the error budget calculated in both percentage and minutes over 30 days, plus a one-paragraph scenario showing how much of that budget a hypothetical incident would consume.

slots.practicalActivity: For the same real service from the last 2 sessions, define its 4 golden signals concretely (the exact metric that represents latency, traffic, errors, and saturation for this specific service). Then write 3 candidate alerts for it, and for each one apply both the "actionable test" and the symptom-vs-cause test from the lesson, rejecting or rewriting any alert that fails either test.
slots.deliverable: A written definition of all 4 golden signals for one real service, plus 3 candidate alerts explicitly evaluated against the actionable test and the symptom-vs-cause test, with any failing alert rewritten until it passes both.

slots.practicalActivity: Sign up for a free Azure account (or use an existing one) and deploy any small free-tier resource (an App Service or a VM). Open Metrics Explorer, chart one of its real platform metrics (CPU percentage or request count) over the last hour, then plot a second metric on the same chart to compare them directly, exactly as the lesson compared response time against request count.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure Metrics Explorer chart from your own deployed resource, showing at least 2 platform metrics plotted together on the same chart.

slots.practicalActivity: Connect your Azure resource to a Log Analytics workspace (enable diagnostic settings if needed) and write a real KQL query against its request or activity table: filter to the last hour, summarize into a 5-minute bin, and render it as a timechart, following the exact pipeline shape (where -> summarize ... by bin() -> render timechart) from the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A real KQL query run against your own Log Analytics workspace using where, summarize ... by bin(), and render timechart, with its chart output.

slots.practicalActivity: Attach Application Insights to a real small web app (even a simple one you deploy for this purpose) and generate some real traffic by clicking through it a few times. Open the Application Map to see your app's real topology, then drill from one node into a specific request's end-to-end transaction details to see every hop it made.
slots.deliverable: A real Application Insights Application Map for your own app, plus one end-to-end transaction detail view drilled into from a map node, showing the hops a specific request made.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real Action Group in your Azure subscription (email notification is enough) and a metric alert rule referencing a real signal from your resource (e.g. average response time or CPU), with a real condition and severity. Trigger it for real if you can (generate load or temporarily lower the threshold) and confirm you actually receive the notification.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure Monitor alert rule with a reusable Action Group attached, with proof (a received email/notification) that it actually fired against your own resource.

slots.practicalActivity: Sign up for a free AWS account and launch any small free-tier resource (an EC2 t2.micro or a Lambda function). In the CloudWatch console, find its namespace and dimensions, chart a real metric, and create one static-threshold alarm against it, watching it sit in INSUFFICIENT_DATA before settling into OK.
slots.deliverable: A real CloudWatch alarm created against your own AWS resource, with a screenshot showing its state transition from INSUFFICIENT_DATA to OK (or ALARM).

slots.practicalActivity: Send your resource's logs into a CloudWatch log group (the default for Lambda, or the CloudWatch agent for EC2), then write a real Logs Insights query using fields, filter, sort, and limit to find your 20 most recent or slowest log entries, followed by a second query using stats ... by bin() to aggregate them into time buckets.
slots.deliverable: Two real CloudWatch Logs Insights queries run against your own log group — one listing filtered/sorted individual entries, one aggregating with stats ... by bin() — with their output.

slots.practicalActivity: Enable X-Ray tracing on your Lambda function or a small instrumented app (the X-Ray SDK quickstart is enough), generate a few real requests, and open the service map to see it rendered automatically from your traces. Click into one specific trace and read its timeline to identify which segment actually took the most time.
slots.deliverable: A real AWS X-Ray service map built from your own traced requests, plus one trace's timeline with the dominant (slowest) segment identified by name and duration.

slots.practicalActivity: Open your AWS account's CloudTrail Event history (already enabled by default, no setup) and filter it to find the actual management events from your own activity this chapter — creating your EC2/Lambda resource, your CloudWatch alarm, your X-Ray configuration. Clear the default read-only filter and use the Event name filter to isolate one specific action you personally took.
slots.deliverable: A real CloudTrail Event history search, with the default filter cleared, isolating one specific management event (by Event name) that you personally triggered earlier in this chapter.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Prometheus locally (binary or Docker) and run it against its own /metrics endpoint with the default config — Prometheus can scrape itself. Confirm in its Targets page that the scrape is succeeding (state UP), and write one sentence explaining why a pull-based system can tell you a target is down when a push-based one can't.
slots.deliverable: A locally running Prometheus instance with its Targets page showing a real successful self-scrape in the UP state, plus a one-sentence explanation of the pull-vs-push detection difference.

slots.practicalActivity: Add the prometheus_client library (or your language's equivalent) to a small app of your own — even a 1-endpoint Flask/Express app — and add a real Counter and a real Histogram exactly like the lesson's checkout example, exposing /metrics. Point your local Prometheus at it and confirm both metrics show up as real scraped data.
slots.deliverable: A small app of your own exposing a real Counter and Histogram via /metrics, confirmed as successfully scraped by your local Prometheus instance.

slots.practicalActivity: Against the metrics from your own instrumented app, write and run 4 real PromQL queries in Prometheus's expression browser: a raw instant vector, a rate() over your counter, a histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) over your histogram, and a sum(...) by (...) aggregation.
slots.deliverable: 4 real PromQL queries (instant vector, rate(), histogram_quantile(), and an aggregation) run against your own app's metrics in Prometheus's expression browser, with their output.

slots.practicalActivity: Install node_exporter on your own machine (or a VM/container) and confirm Prometheus scrapes real host-level metrics like CPU and memory from it. If you have a Kubernetes cluster from an earlier course, deploy kube-state-metrics as well and query one of its metrics (like kube_pod_status_phase) to see real cluster object state.
slots.deliverable: A running node_exporter successfully scraped by Prometheus with real host metrics visible, plus (if a cluster is available) one real kube-state-metrics query result showing actual pod/deployment state.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Grafana locally, add your local Prometheus as a data source, and build a real 4-panel dashboard for your own instrumented app using the exact PromQL from your last 2 sessions: request rate, p95 latency, error rate, and one more panel of your choice.
slots.deliverable: A real Grafana dashboard with at least 4 panels, each backed by a real PromQL query against your own app's metrics, screenshotted or exported as JSON.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Alertmanager locally and wire it to your Prometheus instance. Write one real alerting rule against your own app's metrics (e.g. error rate over a threshold, for: 1m) and a minimal Alertmanager route sending to a free webhook endpoint (webhook.site is fine for testing) or a Slack channel if you have one. Trigger the condition for real and confirm the notification arrives.
slots.deliverable: A real Prometheus alerting rule that fired against your own app's metrics, routed through a working local Alertmanager to a real webhook or Slack notification you can show arrived.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending Prometheus/Grafana lab: run your own small app end to end through the full stack built this chapter — instrumented with a counter and histogram, scraped by Prometheus alongside node_exporter, visualized in a 4-panel Grafana dashboard, with one real Alertmanager-routed alert rule tied to one of those panels. Generate enough traffic or load to make at least one panel visibly move and, if your alert's threshold allows, fire for real.
slots.deliverable: One complete, running local observability stack (your app + node_exporter -> Prometheus -> Grafana dashboard -> Alertmanager) demonstrated together with real traffic moving at least one dashboard panel.

slots.practicalActivity: Convert your own small app's logging (from Chapter 4) from plain text to real structured JSON log lines, with timestamp, level, service, message, and a generated correlation_id on every request. Model two different "services" (even two endpoints pretending to be two services) passing the same correlation ID through a function call, and confirm you can find both log lines by searching for that one ID.
slots.deliverable: Real structured JSON log output from your own app including timestamp, level, service, message, and a correlation ID, with at least 2 log lines sharing one correlation ID across what you've modeled as 2 different services.

slots.practicalActivity: Run Grafana Loki locally (Docker is simplest) alongside Promtail (or the Docker logging driver) shipping your own app's structured logs into it. Write a real LogQL query combining a label selector with a text filter, like {service="yourapp"} |= "error", and confirm it returns your own real log lines.
slots.deliverable: A real LogQL query run against your own app's logs centralized in a local Loki instance, combining a label selector with a text filter, with its actual results.

slots.practicalActivity: Add the OpenTelemetry SDK to your own app and wrap at least one real operation (a call to a database, an external API, or a deliberately slow function) in a span. Export traces to a local Jaeger instance (Docker, one command) and find your own trace in its Find Traces search, then read its waterfall to confirm the span's duration matches what you expected.
slots.deliverable: A real trace from your own app visible in a local Jaeger UI, with its waterfall view showing the specific span you instrumented and its measured duration.

slots.practicalActivity: Tie this chapter together for real: confirm the trace ID OpenTelemetry assigns to a request also appears in that request's structured log line (most OTel SDKs do this with one config line). Simulate the lesson's Northbridge-style investigation yourself — start from a Grafana metrics panel showing a spike (or generate slow requests to fake one), find the matching log line by timestamp, read its trace_id, and jump to that exact trace in Jaeger.
slots.deliverable: A real walkthrough, screenshotted step by step, of going from a metrics spike to a matching structured log line to its exact trace in Jaeger, all tied together by one shared trace ID from your own app.

slots.practicalActivity: Take a real (or realistically simulated) slowdown in your own app from Chapters 4-5 — throttle a dependency call or add an artificial delay — and run the lesson's full 5-step method against it for real: confirm the symptom with a real measured number, check your 4 golden signals, check recent changes (your own last commit/config change), narrow using your real trace, and apply the USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) to the specific resource you suspect.
slots.deliverable: A written incident narrative following the 5-step method against a real (or deliberately simulated) slowdown in your own app, including a real measured symptom number and a USE-method breakdown of the resource you identified as the bottleneck.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a real on-call rotation and escalation policy for a 4-person team (even a hypothetical one) covering your own app, with specific escalation timing. Write a severity rubric (SEV1-SEV4) with concrete criteria specific to your app, and simulate being incident commander for 10 minutes on a real or practice incident, writing a timestamped log of IC-specific coordination actions kept clearly separate from any technical fix actions.
slots.deliverable: A written on-call rotation and escalation policy, an app-specific SEV1-4 rubric, and a timestamped incident-commander action log from a 10-minute simulated incident, kept clearly separate from any technical fix actions.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one real, specific 4-part runbook (trigger, diagnose, remediate, escalate) for the actual slowdown scenario you troubleshot 2 sessions ago in your own app — with real dashboard links or query text in the diagnose section, not placeholders. Then classify one remediation step as a candidate for auto-remediation and a different one as better suited to ChatOps, explaining why for each using the lesson's risk/reversibility reasoning.
slots.deliverable: A real 4-part runbook for your own app's actual troubleshot scenario, with real queries/links in its diagnostic steps, plus a written classification of one remediation step as auto-remediation-worthy and another as ChatOps-worthy, with reasoning.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a full 5-section blameless postmortem for the same real incident you've been working with the last 3 sessions (your own app's slowdown): a timestamped timeline built from your actual logs/metrics, a quantified impact statement, at least one root cause distinct from at least one contributing factor, and 2 real action items each with a specific owner (even if it's just you) and a due date.
slots.deliverable: A complete 5-section postmortem for your own app's real incident, with a quantified impact statement, root cause separated from contributing factors, and at least 2 action items each with a named owner and due date.

slots.practicalActivity: Audit the alert rule you built back in Chapter 4 (the Alertmanager lesson) against this lesson's 4 fixes: is it symptom-based or cause-based, is it actionable, does its severity match real impact, and would it get deduplicated if multiple instances fired it at once? Rewrite it as an SLO-burn-rate alert using the error budget math from Chapter 1, Lesson 3, and compare the old and new alert's expression side by side.
slots.deliverable: A written audit of your own Chapter 4 alert rule against all 4 alert-fatigue fixes, plus a rewritten SLO-burn-rate version of that same alert with its expression shown side by side with the original.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Instrument and Monitor a Service

slots.practicalActivity: Pick your real capstone service (reuse your Chapters 4-5 app if it fits the lesson's sizing guidance, or pick a new small one) and write out the 4 required planning decisions in full: its golden signals named concretely, exactly what you'll instrument and with which specific tools, where metrics/logs will live and how you'll visualize them, and 2-3 plain-English alert conditions.
slots.deliverable: A written capstone plan naming your real service and covering all 4 required planning decisions: concrete golden signals, instrumentation tools, visualization stack, and 2-3 plain-English alert conditions.

slots.practicalActivity: Execute your kickoff plan in the lesson's exact build order: instrument real metrics (a counter, a duration histogram, one saturation metric), switch to structured logs with a correlation ID, wrap your main dependency call in a trace span, build a 4-6 panel dashboard, and finally turn your 2-3 planned alerts into real, working alert rules with real thresholds derived from your own service's observed behavior.
slots.deliverable: A real, running capstone service with metrics, structured logs with correlation IDs, a basic trace span, a 4-6 panel dashboard, and 2-3 working alert rules with thresholds derived from your own service's observed behavior.

slots.practicalActivity: Write your one-page capstone write-up (what the service does, what you instrumented and why, one real decision with its trade-off, what you'd do next) and sketch the simple block-diagram architecture from service through metrics/logs/traces to dashboard and alerts. Practice presenting it out loud in under 2 minutes, then answer your own 3 toughest follow-up questions in writing: how you picked a threshold, what happens on a false positive, and what changes at 10x traffic.
slots.deliverable: A one-page capstone write-up, a block-diagram architecture sketch, and written answers to 3 real follow-up interview questions about your own build's thresholds, false positives, and scaling.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can instrument a real service with metrics, structured logs, and distributed traces; build real Azure Monitor/CloudWatch and Prometheus-plus-Grafana dashboards and alerts tied to SLOs and the four golden signals; correlate a metric spike to its exact root-cause log line and trace; and run a real incident end to end — triage, on-call coordination, a runbook, and a blameless postmortem with owned action items.
